content: Typhoid and paratyphoid fever are bacterial infections that cause febrile illnesses and are prevalent in many lowand middle-income countries. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends fluoroquinolone antibiotics in regions where resistance to older first-line antibiotics is known. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy of fluoroquinolone antibiotics in treating enteric fever in both children and adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, up to February 2011. Randomized controlled trials involving patients with blood, stool, or bone marrow culture-confirmed enteric fever were included. Two authors independently evaluated the methodological quality of the studies and extracted data. Risk ratios (RR) and mean differences were calculated with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The analysis considered factors such as treatment duration, dosage, study year, and levels of antibiotic resistance. A total of 26 studies involving 3033 patients were included in the review. Fluoroquinolones versus older antibiotics (chloramphenicol, co-trimoxazole, amoxicillin, and ampicillin): In a study conducted in Pakistan in 2003-2004, high clinical failure rates were observed with chloramphenicol and co-trimoxazole, although microbiological resistance was not confirmed. A seven-day course of ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin was found to be superior. Older studies comparing fluoroquinolones to these antibiotics did not show significant differences (six trials, 361 participants). However, in smaller studies conducted nearly two decades ago, fluoroquinolones demonstrated fewer clinical failures compared to ampicillin and amoxicillin (two trials, 90 participants, RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.57). Fluoroquinolones versus current second-line options (ceftriaxone, cefalexin, and azithromycin): Two studies compared a seven-day course of oral fluoroquinolones with a three-day course of intravenous ceftriaxone. These studies were too small to detect significant differences between the antibiotics (two trials, 89 participants). In Pakistan in 2003-2004, no clinical or microbiological failures were observed with a seven-day course of ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, or cefixime (one trial, 139 participants). In Nepal in 2005, gatifloxacin was found to reduce clinical failure and relapse rates compared to cefixime, despite a high prevalence of nalidixic acid resistance (NaR) in the study population (one trial, 158 participants, RR 0.04, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.31). In Vietnam between 1998 and 2002, a seven-day course of ofloxacin had a higher rate of clinical failures compared to azithromycin in populations with multi-drug resistance (MDR) and NaR enteric fever (two trials, 213 participants, RR 2.20, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.94). However, a more recent study from Vietnam in 2004-2005 found no significant difference between gatifloxacin and azithromycin, with both drugs performing well (one trial, 287 participants). Conclusions: Fluoroquinolones generally performed well in treating typhoid fever and may be superior to alternative antibiotics in certain settings. However, due to the evolving nature of antibiotic resistance and the small size of many studies, it is difficult to draw definitive conclusions about their comparative effectiveness in contemporary practice. Policymakers and clinicians should consider local resistance patterns when selecting fluoroquinolones or alternative treatments. There is evidence suggesting that gatifloxacin, a newer fluoroquinolone, remains effective in some regions where resistance to older fluoroquinolones has emerged. However, direct comparisons between different fluoroquinolones in these settings are lacking.
